title: Build the per-order table
prompt: Using `items` (revenue column already added), build `per_order`: one row per `order_id` with the columns `revenue` (sum), `lines` (number of order lines) and `units` (sum of `quantity`). Then set `avg_order_value` to the mean order revenue rounded to 2 decimals, `multi_line_share` to the share of orders with 2 or more lines rounded to 3 decimals, and `top_product` to the `product_id` with the highest total revenue.
hints: `items.groupby("order_id").agg(revenue=("revenue", "sum"), ...)` with one keyword per output column.
Count lines with `("order_item_id", "count")` or `("order_id", "size")`. A share is the mean of a boolean: `(per_order["lines"] >= 2).mean()`.
`items.groupby("product_id")["revenue"].sum().idxmax()` returns the label of the largest group.
explanation: Named aggregation turns 3,991 lines into 2,066 orders in one call, with readable column names. The checks confirm the parts add up: the `lines` column sums back to 3,991 and units to the total quantity, so no line was lost or counted twice. Average order value is 228.43 dollars, and 55.1% of orders contain more than one product, a useful fact when someone proposes a promotion on single items. Product 21, the Standing Desk 140cm, is the top earner. `as_index=False` would also be accepted: then `order_id` is a column instead of the index.

checks.shape: `per_order` has 2,066 rows and the columns revenue, lines, units
checks.lines-units: Lines and units add back up to the item table's totals
